t: Valid Subarrays With Matching Sum Digits I
o: Count subarrays whose sum's first digit and last digit both equal x. Since nums[i] >= 1, all sums are positive, so the first digit is obtained by repeatedly dividing by 10 and the last digit is sum % 10. With n <= 1500 there are about 1.1M subarrays, so enumerating all of them with a running sum — O(n^2) total work — easily fits. Example 1 checks [1], [1,100], [100,1], [1] giving 4; Example 2 fails the single check giving 0.
k: A running sum over fixed left endpoints enumerates all subarrays in O(n^2) without a prefix array.
First digit of a positive sum: strip digits with s /= 10 until s < 10; last digit: s % 10.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate all subarrays with running sums
a.i: Fix the left endpoint l and extend r to the right, maintaining the sum incrementally. For each sum, compute its first and last digit in O(log sum) and compare both to x. No data structures are needed; the small constraint (n <= 1500) makes brute force the intended solution.
s: Extend r from l to n-1, adding nums[r] to s.
Compute first digit fd of s; if fd == x and s % 10 == x, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n^2 log S) time — all O(n^2) subarrays, each digit extraction costs O(log sum); O(1) extra space.
a.sp: O(1) — only scalars beyond the input.

w: There is no meaningfully faster asymptotic approach here: the digit condition couples the whole sum, defeating prefix-sum hashing. Use 64-bit sums since n * max(nums[i]) reaches 1.5e12. Edge cases: single-element subarrays (first digit equals the element itself), and x equal to a digit of a multi-digit sum. Follow-up: how would you scale to n = 1e5? You would need digit-structure insights per sum range, likely via grouped prefix sums.
